extracted.intended_audience: speculative-fiction writers (podcast listeners) interested in uplift/anthropomorphism and themes of death
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for creating believable uplifted/anthropomorphic animal characters and societies, and for using speculative devices to explore death and mortality in fiction. Includes worldbuilding, characterization, thematic handling of death, and story-motivating MacGuffins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-human characters to explore the human condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploring the human condition through things that are not human is at the core of science fiction; anthropomorphic animals let you get alien perspectives while remaining familiar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat uplifted animals as a means to examine human attributes — their alienness plus our familiarity gives you leverage. Frame scenes so readers can see aspects of themselves reflected in non-human characters. Anti-pattern: using animals as mere novelty or caricature instead of as tools to investigate human themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground behaviors and societies in real animal ethology
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw on real animal behavior and social structures to inform how uplifted species organize and act (e.g., elephant family units, male bachelor behavior, prairie-dog sentries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research real-world animal behavior and adapt it plausibly to your worldbuilding. Use concrete behavioral details (like a sentry at an opening) to make scenes feel earned and to create believable cultural norms. Example: a prairie-dog colony always leaves a sentry — incorporate that into plot beats. Anti-pattern: inventing behavior divorced from believable animal logic, which can ring false to knowledgeable readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make characters become 'people' — prioritize humanity over physiology
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters stop being animals and become people for readers, the story succeeds; the humanity behind a character matters more than what flesh or DNA they have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on inner life, motivations, and relationships to achieve empathy. Ensure protagonists have recognizable emotional arcs so readers relate regardless of species. Scoring note: a successful uplifted character 'feels' human even if biologically nonhuman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let species-specific social structure shape plot and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Species' social arrangements (housing, family units, movement patterns) should affect story logistics and worldbuilding (e.g., elephant 'family homes' vs bachelor pads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use societal differences to create interesting settings, conflicts, and comic/tragic elements. Example: long-distance traveling males who never stay create transient communities and story opportunities. Anti-pattern: shoehorning human social norms onto nonhuman societies without considering consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small, behavior-based details to give stories traction
rubrics_metrics.description: Animal/alien behavior details provide traction for exploring human attributes — readers recognize authenticity and the story gains depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include evocative small details (grouping animals as they would in the wild, sentries, nesting behavior) to reward attentive readers and deepen immersion. Caution: balance detail so non-experts aren't alienated; subtlety often works better than didactic exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit scale and visual/logistical implications of nonhuman protagonists
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical size and bodily differences (e.g., drawing an elephant versus humans) affect composition, staging, and practical storytelling choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate how scale impacts scenes, panels, choreography, and reader perception. If media is visual (comics, film), plan layouts and scenes with creature scale in mind. Anti-pattern: ignoring scale problems, leading to awkward or unconvincing scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use speculative MacGuffins to concretely explore death and immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a speculative device (e.g., a drug that lets people perceive particles of memory and converse with the dead) as the story engine to interrogate mortality and grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the device meaningful to characters and culture — its rules, scarcity, and consequences should drive conflict and theme. Use it to pose ethical questions (who gets access? who profits?). Anti-pattern: treating the device as mere plot convenience without grounding its social/psychological effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray foreknowledge of death to heighten emotional stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Show characters who know they're approaching the end (e.g., knowing 'this will be the last thing I make') to explore artistic legacy, regret, and life choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes that capture the psychology of 'lastness' — what an artist chooses to make when they know it's their final work, how people spend a last day, what they prioritize or forgo. Example: a character carving a last work of art for someone else and the emotional resonance that creates. Anti-pattern: treating foreknowledge superficially or only for melodrama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore varied behavioral responses to impending death
rubrics_metrics.description: Different people react differently to knowing their end — from hedonism to making peace or completing unfinished tasks — and these choices define character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and dramatize multiple plausible responses (recklessness, reconciliation, quiet acceptance) and let these choices reveal character. Use contrast between reactions to build theme. Writing prompt: 'come up with a method for immortality, then convince your protagonist not to use it' as a way to generate conflict and character revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural rituals and myth (prophecy/destinations) to dramatize death
rubrics_metrics.description: Create cultural practices around death (e.g., waking up knowing your destination island) to make mortality feel embedded and consequential in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent rituals, locations, and myths that shape how societies understand death; these can be plot hooks and sources of mystery. Make sure rituals arise logically from species' sensibilities and constraints. Anti-pattern: arbitrary rituals without connection to society's biology or history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create antagonists motivated by control of mortality technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict can arise from outsiders or institutions wanting access to immortality resources (e.g., abducting someone because 'no one will look for him' once he appears dead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scarcity and incentive structures (profit, power, fear of loss) to explain antagonists' actions and escalate stakes. Ensure antagonist motivations tie back to the central speculative premise rather than feeling tacked-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose narrative voice and performance to enhance theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Format and delivery (e.g., audiobook narrator selection) can deeply affect how the story and its themes of death and personhood land with audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the narrator's tone and presence to the book's emotional core; a well-chosen performer can elevate themes. Consider audio performance as part of storytelling design rather than an afterthought.
